children: Geopolitical tensions, the threat of the US Biosecure Act and growing calls for a "China+1" supply chain strategy have done little to dent demand for Chinese contract research, development and manufacturing organisations (CRDMOs), with industry giant WuXi Biologics reporting a swelling order book and raising its growth outlook.

The bellwether of China's biotech outsourcing industry, WuXi Biologics is closely watched to see if global drugmakers are shifting supply chains, particularly after sister company WuXi AppTec was flagged by the US government for alleged state and military ties, a claim it denies. Its latest results suggest they are not.

The company's performance highlights a stark contrast with Indian contract development and manufacturing organisations (CDMOs), which continue to see strong inquiry pipelines but face difficulties in converting requests for proposals (RFPs) and quotations (RFQs) into commercial contracts. Indian CDMOs have struggled to win any large biologics contract in recent times.
Surge continues

In the first half of FY26, WuXi Biologics posted revenue of RMB 11.8 billion ($1.65 billion), up 18.4 percent from the previous year. Its backlog rose 23 percent to $25.06 billion. WuXi AppTec reported RMB 28.90 billion ($4.05 billion) in 1H26 alone (up 38.9 percent YoY). WuXi AppTec’s order book (backlog for continuing operations) stands at RMB 66.43 billion ($9.35 billion).

"Driven by its 'Follow and Win the Molecule' strategy and a broader industry recovery, WuXi Bio delivered robust 1H26 results," said Cyrus Ng, an analyst at Deutsche Bank Research. "Management raised its FY26 reported revenue growth guidance and expects a 20 percent revenue CAGR over the next three years alongside gross margin expansion."
The order momentum comes despite persistent concerns over US efforts to reduce dependence on Chinese biotech supply chains.
According to a sector update from Deutsche Bank, regulatory pressure on Chinese pharma remains a long-term risk but the near-term impact on business operations has been limited.

"Intermittent escalations in US-China tensions continue to create volatility... we believe the US trajectory toward regulatory action against the Chinese pharmaceutical industry remains clear but near-term impacts on operational momentum remain limited," the bank said.
Not just Wuxi, other Chinese CRDMOs such as such as Pharmaron, Asymchem and Tigermed are also doing well.
Execution prowess
Industry experts say biotech companies continue to prioritise execution, speed and manufacturing scale over geopolitical concerns.

WuXi's network spans research, development and commercial manufacturing, allowing customers to move drug candidates quickly from discovery to market. It has also built significant capabilities in high-growth segments such as antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), peptides, bispecific antibodies and other complex biologics.

By comparison, Indian CDMOs remain focused on small-molecule chemistry and active pharmaceutical ingredients. Their biologics manufacturing capabilities are still developing. Although many global drugmakers are exploring alternatives to China, Indian companies have struggled to secure large late-stage biologics contracts.

"We are seeing an influx of RFQs as Western biopharma companies look for alternative supply chains," said a senior executive at a leading Indian CDMO, requesting anonymity. "However, when it comes to signing actual purchase orders, clients hesitate."

Indian players still lack manufacturing infrastructure and proven commercial track record that WuXi offers. Biotechs cannot afford delays in their clinical timelines, so they end up sticking with Chinese partners.
Heavy investments in R&D, manufacturing

A major factor behind WuXi's dominance is scale. The combined annual revenue of WuXi AppTec and WuXi Biologics exceeds $9 billion, dwarfing the estimated $3 billion-$3.5 billion generated by India's leading CDMO players combined.
The group reinvests into capacity expansion, deploying billions of dollars into biologics, ADC and peptide manufacturing platforms.

Its position is further strengthened by China's growing biotech ecosystem. China's domestic biotech funding has rebounded, helping drive a 51 percent YoY increase in revenue and creating a steady pipeline of projects.

WuXi's role in supplying critical ingredients and components for blockbuster medicines, including Eli Lilly's obesity and diabetes therapies Mounjaro and Zepbound, also shows how difficult it is for global drugmakers to replace the Chinese company.

The much-discussed China+1 shift remains stronger in rhetoric than in execution. Until Indian CDMOs build capacity and establish a track record in manufacturing complex therapies, companies such as WuXi are likely to remain the preferred partners for global biotech innovators.

title: Chinese CDMO WuXi defies China+1 push; Indian CDMOs struggle to win contracts
